notes: Recall item, answered from my own knowledge and written down before the slice was opened: the standard textbook range of the weak nuclear force is of the order of 10⁻¹⁶ m, against about 10⁻¹⁵ m for the strong nuclear force, with the gravitational and electromagnetic forces infinite in range. Matches the solution. The two positive-exponent options are macroscopic and cannot be any force range, and 10⁻¹⁰ m is the size of an atom, not a nuclear-scale range, so option 4 is the only physically possible one. Both printed statements are true: the weak force does act over distances smaller than a nucleus, and its range is smaller than the strong force's. Both common_mistakes entries reproduce and land on the option they name: the atomic-scale confusion gives 10⁻¹⁰ m, option 2, and dropping the minus sign on the exponent gives 10¹⁶ m, option 1. Checked and did not file: option 3 (10¹⁰ m) has no entry, but reaching it needs both named errors stacked together rather than one obvious slip, so this is not a coverage gap. Also not filed, because it is a textbook convention and not a defect in this question: the modern measured range implied by the W boson mass is nearer 10⁻¹⁸ m, while 10⁻¹⁶ m is the value the NCERT fundamental-forces table gives and the only small value the options offer. Difficulty 'easy' is right for a one-line recall. Plain-language pass.
